The edge computing service model would be far more appropriate, as it places computing power at the sensor, minimizing the data that must be sent back to the cloud over limited connectivity network links.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Serverless (FaaS) runs code in the provider's cloud, so the sensor data would still have to go back over the limited link before any processing could happen.
Correct. Edge computing puts processing power at the sensor itself, so images are analyzed locally and only the results travel over the limited network link to the cloud.
Incorrect. IaaS provides virtual machines and infrastructure in the provider's data center. The raw video would have to be sent to the cloud to be processed, which defeats Carl's goal.
Incorrect. SaaS delivers complete applications hosted by the provider, so the data has to be sent to the cloud. It does not put computing power on the remote device.

questions.stem: What action can you take to prevent accidental data disclosure due to wear leveling on an SSD device before reusing the drive?
questions.explanation: Wear leveling is about writing to the disk evenly. Encrypting the data would protect against the disclosure of data on portions of the disk that have remnants due to too much wear and having been set aside as no longer usable. Disk formatting does not effectively remove data from any device. Degaussing is effective only for magnetic media. Physically destroying the drive would not permit reuse.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Reformatting only rewrites file-system structures and doesn't actually remove data on any device. On an SSD it can't reach the worn-out or reserved blocks that wear leveling has set aside.
Correct. Disk encryption keeps the data in remnant blocks unreadable, including blocks that wear leveling retired as unusable. The drive can then be reused without exposing that data.
Incorrect. Degaussing works only on magnetic media. SSDs store data in flash memory cells, so a degausser does nothing to them.
Incorrect. Physical destruction would deal with data remanence, but it ruins the drive. The question requires the SSD to be reused, so this option doesn't fit.

questions.stem: Johnson Widgets strictly limits access to total sales volume information, classifying it as a competitive secret. However, shipping clerks have unrestricted access to order records to facilitate transaction completion. A shipping clerk recently pulled all of the individual sales records for a quarter from the database and totaled them up to determine the total sales volume. What type of attack occurred?
questions.explanation: In an aggregation attack, individual(s) use their access to specific pieces of information to piece together a larger picture that they are not authorized to access.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Social engineering means deceiving or intimidating people into giving up sensitive information. The clerk didn't manipulate anyone. They only used database access they were already allowed to have.

Incorrect. Inference means deducing sensitive information indirectly from what you can see. Here the clerk directly added up authorized records to produce the restricted total, which is aggregation, not deduction.

Correct. Aggregation means combining individual pieces of data you're allowed to see into a larger picture you're not allowed to see. Totaling the quarter's order records to get the classified sales volume is exactly that.
Incorrect. Data diddling means changing data in an unauthorized way, often before or during input. The clerk only read and summed the records and changed nothing.

questions.stem: What physical security control broadcasts false emanations constantly to mask the presence of true electromagnetic emanations from computing equipment?
questions.explanation: While all of the controls mentioned protect against unwanted electromagnetic emanations, only white noise is an active control. White noise generates false emanations that effectively “jam” the true emanations from electronic equipment.
optionNotes: Incorrect. A Faraday cage is a passive TEMPEST control. Its metal mesh enclosure absorbs or blocks emanations so they can't leave the area, but it doesn't broadcast any false signals.
Incorrect. Copper-infused windows are passive shielding. The metal in the glass stops emanations from escaping through windows, but nothing is transmitted to mask the real signals.
Incorrect. Shielded cabling is passive. It keeps emanations from leaking out of cable runs, but it doesn't generate any jamming or decoy signals.
Correct. White noise is the only active control here. It keeps broadcasting false emanations that jam, or hide, the real emanations coming from computing equipment.

questions.stem: In a software-as-a-service cloud computing environment, who is normally responsible for ensuring that appropriate firewall controls are in place to protect the application?
questions.explanation: In a software-as-a-service environment, the customer has no access to any underlying infrastructure, so firewall management is a vendor responsibility under the cloud computing shared responsibility model.
optionNotes: Incorrect. In SaaS the customer can't reach the underlying infrastructure, so its security team has no firewall to configure. The customer stays accountable for its data, but it hands responsibility for infrastructure controls to the provider.
Correct. In SaaS the vendor runs the whole stack, including the network and infrastructure, so under the shared responsibility model firewall management belongs to the vendor.
Incorrect. The customer's networking team would handle firewalls on premises or in IaaS. In SaaS the network sits inside the provider's environment, which the customer can't access.
Incorrect. In SaaS the customer has no infrastructure of its own to manage for the application, so this team has no role in its firewall controls. The vendor handles them.

questions.stem: Alice has read permissions on an object, and she would like Bob to have those same rights. Which one of the rules in the Take-Grant protection model would allow her to complete this operation?
questions.explanation: The grant rule allows a subject to grant rights that it possesses on an object to another subject.
optionNotes: Incorrect. The create rule lets a subject create a new object or subject. Alice isn't creating anything. She wants to pass along a right she already holds.
Incorrect. The remove rule lets a subject delete rights it holds. That takes rights away and doesn't give Bob anything.
Correct. The grant rule lets a subject give another subject the rights it holds on an object. That is exactly Alice passing her read permission to Bob.
Incorrect. The take rule lets a subject take rights from another subject. Bob would have to be the one acting, but in this question Alice is handing the right over.

questions.stem: As part of his incident response process, Charles securely wipes the drive of a compromised machine and reinstalls the operating system (OS) from original media. Once he is done, he patches the machine fully and applies his organization's security templates before reconnecting the system to the network. Almost immediately after the system is returned to service, he discovers that it has reconnected to the same botnet it was part of before. Where should Charles look for the malware that is causing this behavior?
questions.explanation: The system Charles is remediating may have a firmware or BIOS infection, with malware resident on the system board. While uncommon, this type of malware can be difficult to find and remove. Since he used original media, it is unlikely that the malware came from the software vendor. Charles wiped the system partition, and the system would have been rebooted before being rebuilt, thus clearing system memory.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Charles securely wiped the OS partition and reinstalled from original media, so any malware stored there would have been destroyed. It can't explain the reinfection.
Correct. Firmware or BIOS malware lives on the system board, so wiping the drive and reinstalling the OS doesn't remove it. That explains the immediate reinfection. It's uncommon and hard to detect.
Incorrect. Memory is volatile. The system would have been rebooted during the rebuild, which clears any malware held in memory, so memory can't keep an infection alive across a reinstall.
Incorrect. He used original vendor media, so it's unlikely the installation media was carrying the malware. Infected shared media is a known way to spread infections, but it doesn't fit this case.

questions.stem: Lauren implements ASLR to help prevent system compromises. What technique has she used to protect her system?
questions.explanation: Lauren has implemented address space layout randomization, a memory protection methodology that randomizes memory locations, which prevents attackers from using known address spaces and contiguous memory regions to execute code via overflow or stack smashing attacks.
optionNotes: Incorrect. ASLR doesn't encrypt anything. It moves where executables and data are loaded in memory so attackers can't guess addresses. It doesn't make memory contents unreadable.
Incorrect. Mandatory access control is an access-control model in which the system enforces access using labels and clearances. It's about who can reach which objects, not where code sits in memory.
Correct. Address space layout randomization places code and data at random memory locations. Attackers can't count on known addresses, which blocks overflow and stack-smashing exploits.

Incorrect. Discretionary access control is an access-control model in which owners set permissions on their own objects. It has nothing to do with randomizing memory layout to stop buffer overflow exploits.

questions.stem: Alan intercepts an encrypted message and wants to determine what type of algorithm was used to create the message. He first performs a frequency analysis and notes that the frequency of letters in the message closely matches the distribution of letters in the English language. What type of cipher was most likely used to create this message?
questions.explanation: This message was most likely encrypted with a transposition cipher. The use of a substitution cipher, a category that includes AES and 3DES, would change the frequency distribution so that it did not mirror that of the English language. This type of attack, where the attacker only has access to an encrypted message, is also known as a ciphertext-only attack.
optionNotes: Incorrect. A substitution cipher swaps letters for other symbols, so the ciphertext letter frequencies would no longer match normal English. That rules it out here.
Incorrect. AES is a modern cipher that uses substitution. Its output looks statistically random and would not mirror English letter frequencies.
Correct. A transposition cipher only rearranges the order of the original letters. The letters themselves stay the same, so their frequencies still match English.
Incorrect. 3DES is a substitution-based block cipher. It hides plaintext statistics, so frequency analysis would not show an English-like distribution.

questions.stem: In a zero trust network architecture, what component is responsible for making policy decisions based upon rules and external data sources?
questions.explanation: In a zero trust network architecture, the policy engine is responsible for making policy decisions based upon rules and external data sources. It uses a trust algorithm to decide whether to grant, deny, or revoke access, considering factors like identity management, threat intelligence, and security information and event management (SIEM) data. The policy administrator, on the other hand, acts based on the decisions made by the policy engine, establishing or removing communication paths and managing session-specific credentials. The policy enforcement point enforces these decisions by controlling access to resources based on instructions from the policy administrator. Lastly, the subject refers to users, services, or systems that request access or attempt to use rights and is not involved in decision-making.
optionNotes: Correct. The policy engine runs a trust algorithm over rules and external inputs such as identity management, threat intelligence, and SIEM data. It then decides whether to grant, deny, or revoke access.
Incorrect. The policy administrator carries out the engine's decisions. It sets up or tears down communication paths and handles session-specific credentials, but it doesn't make the decision itself.
Incorrect. The policy enforcement point controls access to resources on instructions from the policy administrator. It enforces decisions and doesn't make them.
Incorrect. The subject is the user, service, or system asking for access. It requests access and plays no part in deciding policy.

questions.stem: Grace would like to implement application control technology in her organization. Users often need to install new applications for research and testing purposes, and she does not want to interfere with that process. At the same time, she would like to block the use of known malicious software. What type of application control would be appropriate in this situation?
questions.explanation: The blacklisting approach to application control allows users to install any software they want except for packages specifically identified by the administrator as prohibited. This would be an appropriate approach in a scenario where users should be able to install any nonmalicious software they want to use.
optionNotes: Correct. Blacklisting (deny list) lets users install any software except packages the administrator has specifically prohibited. That blocks known malware without getting in the way of research installs.

Incorrect. Graylisting is not a standard application control model. The term usually refers to email anti-spam, where mail from unknown senders is temporarily deferred. It does not provide a list of blocked malicious software.

Incorrect. Whitelisting allows only applications on an approved list and blocks everything else. Users could not freely install new research software, which is exactly the problem Grace wants to avoid.
Incorrect. Bluelisting is not a recognized application control approach. The standard models are allow lists (whitelisting) and deny lists (blacklisting).

questions.stem: Warren is designing a physical intrusion detection system for use in a sensitive media storage facility and wants to include technology that issues an alert if the communications lines for the alarm system are unexpectedly cut. What technology would meet this requirement?
questions.explanation: Heartbeat sensors send periodic status messages from the alarm system to the monitoring center. The monitoring center triggers an alarm if it does not receive a status message for a prolonged period of time, indicating that communications were disrupted.
optionNotes: Correct. A heartbeat sensor sends periodic status signals to the monitoring center. If those signals stop for too long, the center raises an alarm, so a cut communication line gets detected.
Incorrect. Emanation security (TEMPEST) protects against eavesdropping on electromagnetic signals that equipment leaks. It does not watch the alarm communication path or detect a cut line.

Incorrect. A motion detector picks up movement inside a monitored area. It detects intruders, but it can't tell whether the alarm's communication line still works. Line supervision needs a heartbeat sensor.
Incorrect. A Faraday cage is an enclosure that blocks electromagnetic signals from getting in or out. It is an emanation control and gives no alert when alarm communication lines are cut.

questions.stem:
John and Gary are negotiating a business transaction, and John must demonstrate to Gary that he has access to a system. He engages in an electronic version of the “magic door” scenario shown here. What technique is John using?
[Figure, described in text: the "magic door" illustration: a person stands at the entrance of a looped cave; the two paths around the loop (1 and 2) meet at a locked door at the far side.]
questions.explanation: In a zero-knowledge proof, one individual demonstrates to another that they can achieve a result that requires sensitive information without actually disclosing the sensitive information.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Split knowledge divides a secret among several people so no single person holds all of it, much like M-of-N control. Here John proves he has access without revealing the secret at all, which is a zero-knowledge proof.

Correct. In the magic door (Peggy and Victor) example, the prover shows they can produce a result that needs secret knowledge without disclosing that secret. That is exactly what a zero-knowledge proof is.
Incorrect. "Logical proof" is just a general term for reasoning, not a named cryptographic technique. The cave-and-door scenario is the textbook example of a zero-knowledge proof.
Incorrect. "Mathematical proof" means formally proving a theorem. It is not the cryptographic way of showing you know a secret without revealing it, which is what the magic door illustrates.

questions.stem: After scanning all of the systems on his wireless network, Mike notices that one system is identified as an iOS device running a massively out-of-date version of Apple's mobile operating system. When he investigates further, he discovers that the device is an original iPad and that it cannot be updated to a current secure version of the operating system. What would be the best option for handling this device?
options: Isolate the device on a dedicated wireless network.
Install a firewall on the tablet.
questions.explanation: When operating system patches are no longer available for mobile devices, the best option is typically to retire or replace the device. Building isolated networks will not stop the device from being used for browsing or other purposes, which means it is likely to continue to be exposed to threats. Installing a firewall will not remediate the security flaws in the OS, although it may help somewhat. Finally, reinstalling the OS will not allow new updates or fix the root issue.
optionNotes: Correct. The device can no longer get OS patches, so its vulnerabilities will never be fixed. Retiring or replacing it is the only option that removes the risk at its source.
Incorrect. Putting it on its own wireless network doesn't stop people browsing or otherwise using the device. It stays exposed to threats while the OS flaws remain unpatched.
Incorrect. A firewall on the tablet might help a little, but it does nothing to fix the security flaws in the outdated OS.
Incorrect. Reinstalling puts the same outdated, unsupported OS back on the device. No new updates become available, so the root problem stays.

questions.stem: Tonya believes that an attacker was able to eavesdrop on legitimate HTTPS communications between her users and remote web servers by engaging in a DNS poisoning attack. After conducting DNS poisoning, what technique would an attacker likely use to conduct this eavesdropping?
questions.explanation: In a man-in-the-middle attack, the attacker tricks the user into establishing a connection with the attacker. The attacker then establishes a connection to the legitimate server and relays communications between the two, eavesdropping on the contents. A meet-in-the-middle attack is an attack against cryptographic algorithms that use multiple rounds of encryption. There is no indication in the scenario that the attacker used an exhaustive brute-force attack or a specialized timing attack to achieve their goals.
optionNotes: Correct. DNS poisoning sends users to the attacker's host. The attacker then opens its own connection to the real server and relays traffic in both directions, so it can read everything that passes through. That relay is a man-in-the-middle attack.
Incorrect. A brute-force attack tries every possible key or password until one works. Nothing in the scenario suggests an exhaustive key search; the eavesdropping comes from redirecting the traffic.
Incorrect. A timing attack works out secrets by measuring how long cryptographic operations take, which is a side channel. It has nothing to do with relaying traffic after DNS redirection.
Incorrect. Meet-in-the-middle is a cryptanalytic attack on ciphers that use multiple rounds of encryption, such as double DES. Despite the similar name, it does not intercept network sessions.

questions.stem: Howard is choosing a cryptographic algorithm for his organization, and he would like to choose an algorithm that supports the creation of digital signatures. Which one of the following algorithms would meet his requirement?
questions.explanation: Digital signatures are possible only when using an asymmetric encryption algorithm. Of the algorithms listed, only RSA is asymmetric and supports digital signature capabilities.
optionNotes: Correct. RSA is an asymmetric algorithm. Signing with the private key and verifying with the public key gives digital signature capability, which is what Howard needs.
Incorrect. 3DES is a symmetric block cipher that applies DES three times. Both parties share the same key, so it cannot prove which one signed, and it can't create digital signatures.
Incorrect. AES is a symmetric block cipher (Rijndael) used for bulk encryption. With a shared secret key it gives no nonrepudiation, so it can't produce digital signatures.
Incorrect. Blowfish is a symmetric block cipher designed by Bruce Schneier. Like other shared-key ciphers, it can't create digital signatures, which require an asymmetric key pair.

questions.stem: Laura is responsible for securing her company's web-based applications and wants to conduct an educational program for developers on common web application security vulnerabilities. Where can she turn for a concise listing of the most common web application issues?
questions.explanation: The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) produces an annual list of the top 10 web application security issues that developers and security professionals around the world rely upon for education and training purposes. The OWASP vulnerabilities form the basis for many web application security testing products.
optionNotes: Incorrect. CVE is a public dictionary of individually disclosed vulnerabilities in specific products. It is a huge catalog of specific flaws, not a short list of the most common types of web application issues for teaching developers.
Incorrect. The NSA is a US intelligence agency. It issues some security guidance, but it does not publish the widely used short ranking of common web application vulnerabilities.

Correct. OWASP publishes the Top 10, a short list of the most critical web application security risks. Developers and security staff around the world use it for education and training, and many web app testing tools are built on it.

Incorrect. The Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) focuses on cloud security best practices, such as the Cloud Controls Matrix (CCM) and STAR. It is not the standard source for a list of common web application vulnerabilities.

questions.stem: The Bell-LaPadula and Biba models implement state machines in a fashion that uses what specific state machine model?
questions.explanation: The information flow model applies state machines to the flow of information. The Bell-LaPadula model applies the information flow model to confidentiality, while the Biba model applies it to integrity.
optionNotes: Correct. The information flow model applies state machines to how information moves between levels. Bell-LaPadula uses it for confidentiality and Biba uses it for integrity.

Incorrect. The noninterference model is a separate model. It makes sure actions at a higher security level can't affect or be seen by lower-level subjects. It isn't the flow-based state machine model that Bell-LaPadula and Biba are built on.

Incorrect. Cascading is a composition theory. It describes how input to one system becomes output from another when systems are chained together. It is not the state machine model behind Bell-LaPadula or Biba.

Incorrect. Feedback is a composition theory in which one system's output returns as input to another system. It describes how systems are linked, not the information flow model used by Bell-LaPadula and Biba.

questions.stem: During a third-party vulnerability scan and security test, Danielle's employer recently discovered that the embedded systems that were installed to manage her company's new buildings have a severe remote access vulnerability. The manufacturer has gone out of business, and there is no patch or update for the devices. What should Danielle recommend that her employer do about the hundreds of devices that are vulnerable?
options: Identify a replacement device model and replace every device.
Turn off all of the devices.
Move the devices to a secure and isolated network segment.
Reverse engineer the devices and build an in-house patch.
questions.explanation: The most reasonable choice presented is to move the devices to a secure and isolated network segment. This will allow the devices to continue to serve their intended function while preventing them from being compromised. All of the other scenarios either create major new costs or deprive her organization of the functionality that the devices were purchased to provide.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Swapping out hundreds of devices that were only just installed would cost a great deal. Isolating them deals with the risk for much less money, so full replacement isn't the most reasonable first recommendation.

Incorrect. Turning the devices off removes the vulnerability, but the company also loses the building-management function it bought them for. Isolating them keeps them working while blocking remote compromise.
Correct. Putting the devices on a secure, isolated network segment is a compensating control. They keep doing their job, and the remote access vulnerability can't be reached, with no big new costs.

Incorrect. Reverse engineering the firmware and writing an in-house patch would need specialised skills, time and money. It's also risky, and the result can't be supported. That makes it a major new cost compared with segmentation.

questions.stem: What type of motion detector senses changes in the electromagnetic fields in monitored areas?
questions.explanation: Capacitance motion detectors monitor the electromagnetic field in a monitored area, sensing disturbances that correspond to motion.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Infrared (heat-based) detectors pick up changes in heat or infrared radiation in the area, not disturbances in an electromagnetic field.
Incorrect. Wave pattern detectors send a steady ultrasonic or microwave signal into the area and watch for changes in the reflected pattern. They don't watch an electromagnetic field.
Correct. Capacitance detectors monitor the electromagnetic (electrical or magnetic) field in an area and treat disturbances in it as motion.
Incorrect. Photoelectric detectors sense changes in visible light levels. They're usually used in dark rooms with no windows, not for sensing electromagnetic fields.

questions.stem: Mike has been tasked with preventing an outbreak of malware like Mirai, a botnet that targeted IP-based cameras and routers. What type of systems should be protected in his organization?
questions.explanation: Mirai targeted “Internet of Things” devices, including routers, cameras, and DVRs. As organizations bring an increasing number of devices like these into their corporate networks, protecting both internal and external targets from insecure, infrequently updated, and often vulnerable IoT devices is increasingly important.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Servers weren't Mirai's recruits. In the Dyn attack, DNS servers were the DDoS victims, and the infected bots were IoT devices such as cameras and DVRs.
Incorrect. SCADA systems are industrial control systems that run physical processes like utilities. Mirai went after consumer-grade IP cameras, routers and DVRs, not ICS environments.
Incorrect. Mobile devices such as phones and tablets weren't Mirai's targets. It scanned for internet-connected embedded IoT devices with default or weak credentials.
Correct. Mirai infected IoT devices such as routers, cameras and DVRs. These devices are often insecure and rarely updated, so they need protection to keep them out of botnets.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements is correct about the Biba model of access control?
options: It focuses on protecting objects from integrity threats.
questions.explanation: The Biba model focuses only on protecting integrity and does not provide protection against confidentiality or availability threats. It also does not provide protection against covert channel attacks. The Biba model focuses on external threats and assumes that internal threats are addressed programmatically.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Biba covers integrity only and offers no confidentiality protection. Confidentiality is what Bell-LaPadula handles.
Incorrect. Biba covers integrity, but it does nothing for availability, so this pairing is wrong.
Incorrect. Biba gives no protection against covert channel attacks. It only enforces integrity rules such as no read down and no write up.
Correct. Biba is concerned only with protecting objects from integrity threats, especially external ones, and assumes internal threats are handled programmatically.

questions.stem: In Transport Layer Security, what type of key is used to encrypt the actual content of communications between a web server and a client?
questions.explanation: In TLS, both the server and the client communicate using an ephemeral symmetric session key. They generate this key using the Diffie-Hellman key exchange algorithm and then communicate using it throughout the rest of the session.
optionNotes: Correct. TLS peers derive an ephemeral symmetric session key (e.g., via Diffie-Hellman) and use it to encrypt all session content efficiently.
Incorrect. Clients usually have no certificate or key pair in TLS, and asymmetric keys are too slow for bulk data. The content is encrypted with the symmetric session key.
Incorrect. The server's public key, sent in its certificate, is used for authentication and key establishment during the handshake. It does not encrypt the session content.
Incorrect. The server's private key signs or decrypts handshake material to prove the server's identity. It is never used to encrypt the bulk data exchanged in the session.

questions.stem: Beth would like to include technology in a secure area of her data center to protect against unwanted electromagnetic emanations. What technology would assist her with this goal?
questions.explanation: A Faraday cage is a metal skin that prevents electromagnetic emanations from exiting. It is a rarely used technology because it is unwieldy and expensive, but it is quite effective at blocking unwanted electromagnetic radiation.
optionNotes: Incorrect. A heartbeat sensor checks that a device or communication link is still working (a liveness or tamper check). It does nothing to stop electromagnetic emanations from leaving an area.
Correct. A Faraday cage is a metal skin around an area that stops electromagnetic emanations from getting out. It's expensive and awkward to build, but it blocks unwanted EM radiation very well.
Incorrect. Piggybacking is a physical-access attack, where someone follows an authorized person through a secure entrance. It's a threat, not a control, and has nothing to do with emanations.
Incorrect. WPA2 is a wireless encryption protocol. It protects the content of Wi-Fi traffic, but it doesn't stop electromagnetic signals from leaving the secure area.

questions.stem: In a virtualized computing environment, what component is responsible for enforcing separation between guest machines?
questions.explanation: The hypervisor is responsible for coordinating access to physical hardware and enforcing isolation between different virtual machines running on the same physical platform.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Each guest OS runs inside its own VM and controls only that VM. It can't see or police other guests, so it has no way to keep them apart. Isolation is enforced underneath the guest, by the hypervisor, and VM escape is an attack that breaks out past that boundary.
Correct. The hypervisor, also called the virtual machine monitor (VMM), coordinates access to the physical hardware and enforces isolation between the VMs that share a platform.

Incorrect. A kernel is the core of a single operating system and enforces separation between processes inside that OS. Separating whole guest VMs is the job of the hypervisor, which creates, manages and runs the VMs.
Incorrect. "Protection manager" is not a standard virtualization component. The study guide names the hypervisor/VMM as the part that creates and manages VMs and provides isolation between them.

questions.stem: Rick is an application developer who works primarily in Python. He recently decided to evaluate a new service where he provides his Python code to a vendor who then executes it on their server environment. What type of cloud computing environment is this service?
questions.explanation: Cloud computing systems where the customer only provides application code for execution on a vendor-supplied computing platform are examples of platform-as-a-service (PaaS) computing.
optionNotes: Incorrect. With SaaS, the vendor delivers a finished application for the customer to use. Rick is supplying his own code to be run, so this isn't SaaS.
Correct. Rick only supplies application code, and the vendor provides the platform that runs it: hardware, operating system and Python runtime. That is the definition of PaaS.
Incorrect. With IaaS, the vendor provides servers, storage and networking, and the customer installs and manages the operating system and runtime. Rick isn't managing any of that, so this isn't IaaS.

Incorrect. Containers as a Service (CaaS) is for deploying and running containers that the customer builds and manages. Rick is handing over raw code to be run on a vendor platform, not managing containers.

questions.stem: A component failure in the primary HVAC system leads to a high temperature alarm in the data center that Kim manages. After resolving the issue, what should Kim consider to prevent future issues like this?
options: Relocating the data center to a colder climate
questions.explanation: A well-designed data center should have redundant systems and capabilities for each critical part of its infrastructure. That means that power, cooling, and network connectivity should all be redundant. Kim should determine how to ensure that a single system failure cannot take her data center offline.
optionNotes: Incorrect. A closed loop chiller is just another type of cooling unit. If it's the only one, it is still a single point of failure, so a component failure could cause the same overheating again.

Correct. Redundant cooling removes the single point of failure. If one HVAC component fails, another system keeps the data center cool, matching the book's point that power, cooling and network should all be redundant.

Incorrect. Swamp (evaporative) coolers are another cooling technology that adds humidity and works poorly in a data center. Swapping in a different single system does not fix the single-point-of-failure problem.

Incorrect. Moving to a colder climate is costly and impractical. Equipment can still overheat if the only cooling system fails, so it does not give the resilience that removing the single point of failure provides.

questions.stem: Tommy is planning to implement a power conditioning UPS for a rack of servers in his data center. Which one of the following conditions will the UPS be unable to protect against if it persists for an extended period of time?
questions.explanation: UPSs are designed to protect against short-term power losses, such as power faults. When they conduct power conditioning, they are also able to protect against sags and noise. UPSs have limited-life batteries and are not able to maintain continuous operating during a sustained blackout.
optionNotes: Incorrect. A fault is a momentary loss of power. That is exactly the kind of short outage a UPS battery is built to cover, so it isn't the condition a UPS fails against.

Correct. A blackout is a long-term total loss of power. UPS batteries only last a limited time, usually minutes, so they can't keep servers running through a sustained blackout. That needs a generator.
Incorrect. A sag is a brief drop in voltage. A UPS that does power conditioning cleans up the incoming power and smooths out sags, so it does protect against this.
Incorrect. Noise is electrical interference on the power line. A UPS's power-conditioning function filters it out, so noise is a condition the UPS can handle.

questions.stem: Which one of the following humidity values is within the acceptable range for a data center operation?
questions.explanation: Data center humidity should be maintained between 20% and 80%. Values below this range increase the risk of static electricity, while values above this range may generate moisture that damages equipment.
optionNotes: Incorrect. 0% humidity is far below the 20% minimum. Air that dry creates a serious risk of static electricity that can damage equipment.
Incorrect. 10% is below the acceptable 20–80% range. At that level, static electricity discharge becomes a real risk.
Incorrect. 15% is close to the range but still below the 20% lower limit, so the risk of static buildup goes up.
Correct. 40% falls inside the recommended 20–80% data center humidity range. It is dry enough to avoid condensation damage and humid enough to limit static.

questions.stem: Kristen's organization suffered a ransomware infection and has lost access to critical business data. She is considering paying the ransom to regain access to her data. Which of the following statements about this payment are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: Payment of the ransom may be illegal.
Payment of the ransom may result in further demands for payments.
Payment of the ransom guarantees access to the decryption key.
Payment of the ransom may cause a data breach.
questions.explanation: Payment of a ransom often results in the release of a decryption key, but this is not guaranteed by any means. There is also no link between the payment of a ransom and a future data breach, as an attacker may choose to release confidential information regardless of whether the ransom was paid. Depending upon applicable jurisdictions, payment of a ransom may be illegal under corrupt practices laws or embargoes against terrorist organizations. For example, the U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an advisory in 2020 stating that ransom payments may violate sanctions. Payment of a ransom may also cause attackers to consider the victim a “mark” and demand future payments in exchange for continued access to their data.
optionNotes: Correct. Depending on jurisdiction, paying a ransom can break corrupt-practices laws or sanctions and embargoes. OFAC's 2020 advisory, for example, warned that ransom payments may violate sanctions.
Correct. Once a victim pays, attackers may treat them as a 'mark' and keep demanding money in exchange for continued access to the data.
Incorrect. Paying often gets a decryption key released, but there is no guarantee. Criminals have no obligation to deliver the key, and it may not work.
Incorrect. Paying a ransom doesn't cause a breach. An attacker may leak confidential data whether or not the ransom is paid, so the two aren't linked.

questions.stem: Alex's employer creates most of their work output as PDF files. Alex is concerned about limiting the audience for the PDF files to those individuals who have paid for them. What technology can he use to most effectively control the access to and distribution of these files?
questions.explanation: Alex can use digital rights management technology to limit use of the PDFs to paying customers. While DRM is rarely a perfect solution, in this case, it may fit his organization's needs. EDM is electronic dance music, which his customers may appreciate but which won't solve the problem. Encryption and digital signatures can help to keep the files secure and to prove who they came from but won't solve the rights management issue Alex is tackling.
optionNotes: Incorrect. EDM is electronic dance music, not a security technology. It can't limit who views or shares the PDFs.
Incorrect. Encryption keeps files confidential, but once a paying customer decrypts a PDF, it doesn't control further use or redistribution. It isn't a rights-management solution.
Incorrect. Digital signatures prove who created a file and that it hasn't been altered. They don't restrict who can open or share the PDFs.
Correct. Digital rights management (DRM) enforces usage rights on content, limiting access and distribution of the PDFs to paying customers. It isn't perfect, but it fits Alex's need.

questions.stem: As part of his team's forensic investigation process, Matt signs out drives and other evidence from an evidence storage facility before working with them. What type of documentation is he creating?
questions.explanation: Matt is helping to maintain the chain of custody documentation for his electronic evidence. This can be important if his organization needs to prove that the digital evidence they handled has not been tampered with. A better process would involve more than one person to ensure that no tampering was possible.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Criminal is a type of investigation or case, not a kind of documentation. Signing evidence in and out of storage is evidence-handling documentation, whatever kind of case it supports.
Correct. Recording each sign-out of evidence keeps the chain of custody, which proves the digital evidence was not tampered with. Having more than one person involved would make the process stronger.
Incorrect. Civil is an investigation or case type, and it uses the preponderance-of-evidence standard. It is not a form of documentation for tracking who handles evidence.
Incorrect. CYA ("cover your assets") is slang for protecting yourself, not a formal type of forensic documentation. The formal term for tracking evidence possession is chain of custody.

questions.stem: Todd believes that a digital certificate used by his organization has been compromised, and he wants to add it to the certificate revocation list (CRL). What element of the certificate goes on the CRL?
questions.explanation: The certificate revocation list contains the serial numbers of digital certificates issued by a certificate authority that have later been revoked.
optionNotes: Correct. A CRL lists the serial numbers of certificates the CA issued and later revoked, so each revoked certificate is identified by its serial number.
Incorrect. Revocation does end trust in the public key, but the CRL doesn't list public keys. It names revoked certificates by serial number, which is shorter and unique within each CA.
Incorrect. The CA signs the CRL as a whole so people can trust it. The individual certificates' signatures aren't what gets listed; entries are serial numbers.
Incorrect. A compromised private key is often why a certificate gets revoked, but private keys are never published. Putting one on a public CRL would expose it even further.

questions.stem: Alison is examining a digital certificate presented to her by her bank's website. Which one of the following requirements is not necessary for her to trust the digital certificate?
options: She knows that the server belongs to the bank.
She verifies that the certificate is not listed on a CRL.
She verifies the digital signature on the certificate.
questions.explanation: The point of the digital certificate is to prove to Alison that the server belongs to the bank, so she does not need to have this trust in advance. To trust the certificate, she must verify the CA's digital signature on the certificate, trust the CA, verify that the certificate is not listed on a CRL, and verify that the certificate contains the name of the bank.
optionNotes: Correct. Proving the server belongs to the bank is the whole purpose of the certificate, so Alison doesn't need to know this beforehand. The certificate gives her that trust.
Incorrect. This is required. A certificate is only as trustworthy as the CA that issued and signed it. If Alison doesn't trust the CA, its vouching for the bank's identity means nothing to her.

Incorrect. This is required. Alison must check that the certificate doesn't appear on a certificate revocation list (CRL), because a revoked certificate, for example one with a compromised key, can no longer be trusted.
Incorrect. This is required. Checking the CA's digital signature on the certificate proves the certificate is authentic and hasn't been altered since the CA signed it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is an example of a covert timing channel when used to exfiltrate information from an organization?
options: Posting a file on a peer-to-peer file sharing service
Typing with the rhythm of Morse code
Writing data to a shared memory space
questions.explanation: Covert channels use surreptitious communications' paths. Covert timing channels alter the use of a resource in a measurable fashion to exfiltrate information. If a user types using a specific rhythm of Morse code, this is an example of a covert timing channel. Someone watching or listening to the keystrokes could receive a secret message with no trace of the message left in logs.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Email is an ordinary, overt communication channel. It leaves logs and doesn't encode data by changing the timing of a resource, so it isn't a covert timing channel.
Incorrect. Posting a file to a P2P service is an overt way to move data. Nothing is signalled by changing how fast or how often a system resource is used, so it isn't a timing channel.

Correct. Typing in a Morse code rhythm changes the timing of a resource in a way someone else can measure. A person watching or listening to the keystrokes gets the message, and nothing shows up in the logs.
Incorrect. Writing data to a shared memory area where another process can read it is a covert storage channel, not a timing channel.

questions.stem: Which one of the following would be a reasonable application for the use of self-signed digital certificates?
questions.explanation: Self-signed digital certificates should be used only for internal-facing applications, where the user base trusts the internally generated digital certificate.
optionNotes: Incorrect. A digital commerce site serves outside customers, and their browsers won't trust a self-signed certificate. A public site like this needs a certificate from a trusted public CA so customers can verify its identity.

Incorrect. A banking application is public-facing and handles sensitive money transactions, so customers need a certificate signed by a trusted CA. A self-signed certificate can't prove the bank's identity to outside users.

Correct. An internal scheduling application is used only inside the organization, where users can trust the internally generated self-signed certificate. That's the only setting where self-signed certificates fit.

Incorrect. A customer portal is used by outside parties who have no reason to trust the organization's self-signed certificate. They would get browser warnings, so the portal needs a certificate signed by a trusted CA.

questions.stem: Ron is investigating a security incident that took place at a highly secure government facility. He believes that encryption keys were stolen during the attack and finds evidence that the attackers used dry ice to freeze an encryption component. What type of attack was likely attempted?
questions.explanation: In a fault injection attack, the attacker attempts to compromise the integrity of a cryptographic device by causing some type of external fault. For example, they might use high-voltage electricity, high or low temperature, or other factors to cause a malfunction that undermines the security of the device. Side-channel attacks seek to use information about system activity and retrieve information that is actively being encrypted. Brute-force attacks attempt every possible valid combination for a key or password. In a timing attack, the attacker measures precisely how long cryptographic operations take to complete, gaining information about the cryptographic process that may be used to undermine its security.
optionNotes: Incorrect. A side-channel attack passively watches system activity, such as power use or emissions, to pull out data being encrypted. Freezing the device with dry ice actively causes a fault, so this is not side-channel monitoring.
Incorrect. A brute-force attack tries every possible key or password combination. It does not involve physically tampering with hardware or changing its temperature.
Incorrect. A timing attack measures exactly how long cryptographic operations take in order to infer secrets. Freezing a component is not a way of measuring timing.
Correct. A fault injection attack uses an outside stress, such as extreme temperature (here, dry ice) or high voltage, to make the device malfunction and weaken its cryptographic security.

questions.stem:
Match the following numbered security models with the appropriate lettered security descriptions:
Security models:
1. Clark-Wilson
2. Bell-LaPadula
3. Biba

(Arrange the options in the order of the numbered items 1–3.)
options: This model blocks lower-classified objects from accessing higher-classified objects, thus ensuring confidentiality.
The * property of this model can be summarized as “no write-up.”
This model uses security labels to grant access to objects via transformation procedures and a restricted interface model.
questions.explanation:
The security models match with the descriptions as follows:
1. Clark-Wilson: C. This model uses security labels to grant access to objects via transformation procedures and a restricted interface model.
2. Bell-LaPadula: A. This model blocks lower-classified objects from accessing higher-classified objects, thus ensuring confidentiality.
3. Biba: B. The * property of this model can be summarized as “no write-up.”
optionNotes: Goes with item 2, Bell-LaPadula. It is a confidentiality model that stops lower-cleared subjects from reading higher-classified objects (no read-up).

Goes with item 3, Biba. Biba's * (integrity) property means "no write-up": lower-integrity subjects can't write to higher-integrity objects. Bell-LaPadula's * property is the opposite, "no write-down".
Goes with item 1, Clark-Wilson. That model controls access through transformation procedures and a restricted interface (the access triple), so subjects never reach constrained data items directly.

questions.stem:
Match each of these following numbered architecture security concepts with the appropriate lettered description:
Architectural security concepts:
1. Time of check
2. Covert channel
3. Time of use
4. Maintenance hooks
5. Parameter checking
6. Race condition

(Arrange the options in the order of the numbered items 1–6.)
options: A method used to pass information over a path not normally used for communication
The exploitation of the reliance of a system's behavior on the sequence of events that occur externally
The time at which the subject checks whether an object is available
The time at which a subject can access an object
An access method known only to the developer of the system
A method that can help prevent buffer overflow attacks
questions.explanation:
The architecture security concepts match with the descriptions as follows:
1. Time of check: C. The time at which the subject checks whether an object is available
2. Covert channel: A. A method used to pass information over a path not normally used for communication
3. Time of use: D. The time at which a subject can access an object
4. Maintenance hooks: E. An access method known only to the developer of the system
5. Parameter checking: F. A method that can help prevent buffer overflow attacks
6. Race condition: B. The exploitation of the reliance of a system's behavior on the sequence of events that occur externally
optionNotes: Goes with item 2, covert channel. A covert channel moves information over a path that isn't normally used for communication, which gets around the security policy.
Goes with item 6, race condition. A race condition exploits the fact that a system's behavior depends on the order or timing of outside events, as TOCTOU attacks do.
Goes with item 1, time of check. This is the moment the subject checks whether an object is available, before it actually uses it.
Goes with item 3, time of use. This is the moment the subject actually accesses the object. A gap between check and use is what TOCTOU attacks exploit.
Goes with item 4, maintenance hooks. These are back-door entry points known only to the developer, and they can bypass normal access controls.
Goes with item 5, parameter checking. Checking input length and type helps prevent buffer overflow attacks.
